sections.body: The source defines shadercoding through the shader itself: a GPU-directed program involved in the rendering pipeline. Its taxonomy of vertex, tessellation, geometry, and fragment shaders gives readers a concrete account of where code enters image production. This matters because the later art argument depends on treating code as the actual medium of visual formation, not as a hidden support tool.
sections.heading: Technical Object Of Study

sections.body: The authors emphasize fragment shaders because they convert pixel positions into colors and can use formulas, time variables, and external inputs to generate animated images. That framing makes shadercoding legible as a generative practice: the image is computed from mathematical relations, and interaction can be incorporated into the same visual procedure.
sections.heading: Fragment Shaders As Generators

sections.body: Raymarching is presented as the technique that lets fragment shaders recover 3D depth. The source explains the procedure in terms of distance functions, rays launched per pixel, stepwise traversal, and encounters with objects described by signed distance fields. This supports the claim that mathematical scene descriptions can produce complex real-time visual spaces.
sections.heading: Raymarching And Spatial Depth

sections.body: The article repeatedly rejects a simple opposition between technical constraint and creative expression. Mathematical fluency, spatial reasoning, vector operations, and shader language mastery are treated as conditions of artistic agency. In this account, the artist gains expressive freedom not by avoiding technical systems, but by understanding them deeply enough to improvise inside them.
sections.heading: Technique As Artistic Condition

sections.body: Shader Showdowns supply the article's clearest institutional performance frame: a public, timed event where participants code a shader effect in roughly half an hour and are judged on image, code technique, and visual evolution. The visibility of writing code makes the procedure itself part of the artwork's reception, alongside the generated image.
sections.heading: Live Coding As Performance Frame

sections.body: The source is strongest as conceptual and practice-based analysis. Its evidence includes technical definitions, procedural descriptions, cited aesthetic theory, event formats, and first-person accounts from Revision 2016 and 2018. It does not provide quantitative audience data or comparative studies, so broad claims about digital-art performance should be read as argued interpretation rather than measured generalization.
sections.heading: Evidence And Limits

source_dossier.summary_long: Florine Fouquart and Chu-Yin Chen present shadercoding as a practice located at the junction of GPU programming, mathematics, computer graphics, and performance art. The article begins with a technical introduction: shaders are GPU programs that participate in rendering, fragment shaders map pixel positions to colors, and mathematical formulas can generate patterns, animation, and interactivity. Raymarching receives particular attention because it lets a fragment shader recover three-dimensional depth by casting rays through distance-field descriptions of space, making complex forms and repeated spaces available in real time. This technical exposition is not an end in itself. The authors use it to question the figure of the digital artist as a technical artist whose aesthetic choices are formed through scientific and mathematical processes. The article then shifts into a practice-based reflection on live coding, especially Shader Showdown events where participants write visual shader effects in 25 or 30 minutes before an audience. The source argues that constraint, visibility, and time pressure can become generative. Rather than separating technique from expression, the authorial account describes technical mastery as the condition that allows improvisation, bodily absorption, and dialogue with spectators. The strongest evidence is explanatory and experiential: a shader pipeline taxonomy, descriptions of fragment-shader and raymarching procedures, a concrete vector-math lighting example, the judging structure of Shader Showdowns, and a first-person account of reaching the Revision 2018 final. The result is a source best read as theoretical-practical commentary rather than empirical validation. It establishes a vocabulary for understanding shadercoding as art, but its general claims about performance rest on reflective experience, cited aesthetic theory, and examples from live-coding culture rather than systematic audience or practitioner study.
source_dossier.summary_short: Fouquart and Chen frame shadercoding as both GPU graphics technique and live digital-art practice. They explain fragment shaders, raymarching, distance fields, and mathematical image generation, then connect those techniques to Shader Showdown performance. The source argues that technical mastery and constraint can enable expressive real-time improvisation.
